tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.content:
List everything recorded about one discobox as one timeline, newest first.
With --follow, print the last --limit oldest first and keep printing records as
they are recorded.

SOURCE says which trail a record came from, and that is also what says how much
it is worth:

  http   the pool's proxy recorded the request from what crossed the wire. The
         discobox cannot alter it.
  dns    the pool recorded a name the discobox looked up, and what came back.
         The discobox cannot alter it. Read only when --source names it:
         lookups outnumber everything else.
  creds  the server recorded that a credential was issued with this verdict.
         A record marked "report" instead of "use" is one the discobox sent
         after a denial, on its own; the verdict's words are its account
         either way.
  refresh
         the server asked for a new value of a token this discobox needed,
         and recorded who answered and when. How the value was made is the
         answering client's word: its record is marked "client" with -o json.
  hooks  what the coding harness published inside the discobox.
  execs  what the discobox recorded about its own execs.

The hooks and execs trails are kept inside the discobox, where anything running
in it can rewrite them, and can be read only while it runs. A trail that could
not be read is named on stderr (and under unavailable with -o json); its records
are missing from the timeline.

content.text:
Your work is gone, and the repair didn't cause it. The sandbox's data had already been deleted from disk before you clicked repair. Repair found nothing to keep and built a fresh box from the original spec.

**What the sandbox looks like now**
- It's on your local `beenie` server, in the Default pool.
- Its whole folder on the pool, `…/pools/pool_nkzh9kht996k7xb5/sandboxes/sbx_fepr7496gy6bmvty`, was created at 19:41:57 UTC today (12:41:57 your time), the moment of the repair. A sandbox made on Sept 4 should have a folder dated Sept 4.
- The code is at the original commit `225887b`, 538 commits behind, with no changes. Claude was launched again with the original prompt instead of resuming, and `~/.claude` has only a new `history.jsonl`.
- Nothing else from before today exists for it: no other copy on the pool, no recorded network traffic before 19:42 today, and no `refs/discobox/apply/sbx_fepr…` ref or image-paste commit in your local repo.

**Why the repair isn't the cause**
Repair tears down the container (`ArchiveSandbox`, `pool-agent/sandboxruntime/archive.go:77`), keeps the data folder, then rebuilds. Archive never deletes the folder, and if the folder is already missing it just returns NotFound. Since the folder was created during the repair, it didn't exist when the repair started.

**What most likely deleted it**
Only three places in the pool agent can delete a sandbox folder: purging the sandbox, cleaning up a failed restore, and a background reaper. You didn't purge it, and it was never restored, so the reaper is the likely one:

1. Rebuilding a box on a new image or changed settings removes the old container before building the new one (`runtime.go`, the spec-change path in `CreateSandbox`). This box had been rebuilt 127 times, which is normal in the dev loop as images change. If one of those builds fails, the sandbox goes into error with **no container at all**.
2. The reaper (`reapDeadSandboxVolumes`, `runtime.go`) treats any sandbox folder without a container as abandoned. It marks the folder, then deletes it after 24 hours (`sandboxVolumeRetention`). The only folders it skips are deliberately archived ones; it never asks the server whether the sandbox still exists.

So this box sat in error with no container for more than a day, and the reaper deleted its data even though the server still listed it as present.

I can't give the exact time it was deleted. The pool agent's logs start at 05:06 UTC today, when the pool restarted, and the dev server only logs to its terminal. The pattern matches across the pool, though: `sbx_8nnmj…`, `sbx_kcyv2…`, `sbx_jnpa8…`, `sbx_p7ted…` (all in error) and `sbx_6f5c8…` (listed as ready) have neither a container nor a data folder. They've almost certainly lost their data the same way.

**Can it be recovered?** Not through discobox. The only option left is a backup or snapshot of the WSL disk, if you keep one.

**The fix:** the reaper shouldn't delete the data of a sandbox the server still has a record for. A failed rebuild should also keep the data protected, the way an archive does, rather than leaving it to the reaper. Should I write that up and implement it?

- `archive` removes the container and the sandbox's proxy material, keeps
  `data/config/secrets/sources`, and writes a `.discobox-archived` marker.
- `delete` removes all of it, including the durable tree, and confirms.
- `create` clears the marker, which is the whole of what unarchiving needs here:
  the reuse-the-existing-tree path already restores the sandbox.

The marker is what makes retained data legible as retained. On disk an archived
sandbox and one whose container was lost out of band are the same shape, and
only the marker separates "held by intent" from "garbage awaiting the reaper".

### The durable tree travels

`GET`/`PUT .../sandboxes/{id}/tree` (`sandboxruntime/tree.go`) are the two halves
of moving a discobox to another server (ADR 0123). They deal only in the tree:
level-triggered sweep that reclaims the material of sandboxes that no longer
have a container here. That is only about reclaiming disk; sandbox loss travels
on the state channel.

The runtime reaps its own dead sandboxes' persistent volume trees
(`pools/{pool_id}/sandboxes/{sandbox_id}`) on the same backstop, keeping each for
a 24h retention window after it is first seen dead (a tombstone starts the
clock). That window is accident recovery — a container removed out of band or
lost while the pool was down — and covers only what never runs through
`delete`. Archived trees are skipped entirely: deliberate retention is a
control-plane policy with a per-project length the agent does not know, enforced
by an explicit `delete` when it expires (ADR 0022 §4).

All per-sandbox state is project- and pool-scoped by path — sandbox
volume trees live under `projects/{project_id}/pools/{pool_id}/` and proxy
material under `proxy/projects/{project_id}/pools/{pool_id}/` — so agents
sharing a host daemon never reap each other's data. Both trees carry the same
scoping because a reaper's scan must not be wider than the authority it is
given (see `pool-sync` below); the shared per-host CA material and client
certificates stay outside them, keyed by globally unique sandbox ID.

sandbox is skipped, never blocking or failing the rest of the tick, and a poll
or push failure never affects sandbox lifecycle. The bearer token for each

input.content:
Fix: the pool agent's volume reaper deletes the durable tree of a sandbox the control plane still holds.

## What happened (real incident, sbx_fepr7496gy6bmvty on a Docker pool)

A discobox the server still had as `desired_state=present` lost its whole durable
tree (`projects/{project}/pools/{pool}/sandboxes/{sbx}` — home dir, sources,
Claude session). The user hit "repair" on it while it was in an error state;
repair rebuilt it from the original spec (source at the original commit, harness
launched fresh with the original prompt instead of `--resume`). The rebuilt
tree's birth time is the moment of the repair, so the old tree was already gone
before repair ran — repair's `ArchiveSandbox` never deletes the tree and returns
NotFound when it is missing. Several other present sandboxes on the same pool
(mostly `failed`, one `ready`) likewise have neither a container nor a tree.

## Root cause

The chain, all code as it stands on main:

1. `CreateSandbox` (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/runtime.go`) on a spec drift
   (re-pin, harness config change, etc. — this sandbox was at generation 127)
   removes the existing container *before* building the new one. If the build
   fails, the sandbox is left with a tree and no container, and the reconciler
   records a settled failure.
2. A settled failure is converged by design (`ensure` in
   `server/internal/resources/sandboxes/reconciler.go` returns early on
   `Converged() && ErrorMessage != nil`), so nothing recreates the container
   until a user repairs it. That part is intended (ADR 0017 §4).
3. `reapDeadSandboxVolumes` (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/runtime.go`) decides a
   tree is dead purely from the pool agent's local view: no container with that
   sandbox ID → tombstone → `os.RemoveAll` 24h later. The only exemption is the
   `.discobox-archived` marker. The reaper never consults the control plane, so
   "the server holds this sandbox and is waiting on the user" is
   indistinguishable from "garbage", and the data is deleted while the server
   still lists the sandbox.

The design premise in `pool-agent/DESIGN.md` ("covers only what never runs
through `delete`" / accident recovery) is the defect: container absence is not
evidence the sandbox is gone. The agent is not the authority on which sandboxes
exist; the control plane is. ADR 0022 already moved deletion to an explicit,
confirmed `DeleteSandbox` that removes the tree, so a tree whose sandbox the
control plane deleted is already reclaimed without the reaper.

## The fix

Make the control plane the authority for reaping sandbox trees, the same way
`pool-sync` is already the authority for reaping whole pools (see the
`pool-sync` section of `pool-agent/DESIGN.md`: the control plane POSTs the
authoritative set of known pool IDs and the agent reaps only what is outside
it). Concretely:

- The pool agent must never reap a sandbox tree because its container is
  missing. It may reap a tree only when the control plane's authoritative set of
  sandboxes for this pool does not contain it (keep a retention window after
  that, as accident recovery against a bad/partial set). No set received yet →
  reap nothing.
- Deliver that set from the control plane — extend the existing pool-sync path
  or add an equivalent; pick whatever fits the existing model best, and keep the
  set exactly as wide as the tree it authorizes (pool-scoped), per the scoping
  rule already in the DESIGN.md. Every sandbox row not purged (present, archived,
  failed, mid-delete until DeleteSandbox confirms) is in the set.
- Delete the container-absence tombstone logic rather than keeping it as a
  fallback. The archive marker remains for what it is used for besides the
  reaper (refusing on-demand start).
- Also consider whether `CreateSandbox`'s spec-drift path should avoid leaving a
  container-less tree on a failed build at all; fix it if it is a clean change,
  but the reaper authority is the fix that matters.

Follow the repo's process (CLAUDE.md): read DESIGN.md/REVIEW.md root-down for
pool-agent and server/internal/resources/sandboxes; this reverses a stated
premise of ADR 0022 §4 ("the reaper stays, unchanged in purpose"), so write a
Proposed ADR for the decision (rejected alternative: keep container-absence
reaping with a marker for failed sandboxes — rejected because the agent still
would not be the authority and any other container-loss path would lose data),
then implement against it, update the affected DESIGN.md files, and add tests:
a present-but-failed sandbox with no container keeps its tree indefinitely; a
tree whose sandbox is absent from the authoritative set is reaped after
retention; no set → nothing reaped. Run `go tool task check-hooks` before you
finish.

## Why the data was deleted while the server still knew about the sandbox

The pool agent never asks the server which sandboxes exist. Its reaper (`reapDeadSandboxVolumes`) looks only at containers on its own Docker daemon. No container for a sandbox means "dead", the reaper starts a 24h clock, then deletes the folder. The only thing it skips is a folder marked as archived. Whether the server still has the sandbox never enters into it.

The reaper was built for accidents, such as a container removed by hand or lost while the pool was down. But "no container" doesn't mean "no sandbox", and the server already makes containerless sandboxes on its own:

1. **A rebuild removes the old container first.** When a box's settings or image change (yours had been rebuilt 127 times), `CreateSandbox` removes the old container before building the new one. If the build fails, the box has a data folder and no container.
2. **The server waits on purpose.** It records the failure and stops retrying until someone acts, which is what "repair" is for. So the box stays in error with no container.
3. **The reaper deletes it.** It sees a folder with no container and no archived marker, and deletes it 24h later. The server still lists the box as present.

The folder is also unnecessary for cleaning up deleted boxes. Since ADR 0022, deleting a sandbox removes its folder directly and confirms it. The reaper's real job had become catching leftovers no server holds anymore, and the pool agent was judging that without asking the one component that knows.

## The fix I asked for

- **Make the server the authority**, as it already is for whole pools. Today the server sends the pool agent the full list of pools that exist, and the agent cleans up only what's outside that list. The same should apply to sandboxes: the server sends each pool its full list of sandboxes, covering present, failed, archived, and still-being-deleted ones. The agent may delete a folder only when its sandbox isn't on that list, after a grace period. If it hasn't received a list yet, it deletes nothing.
- **Remove the "no container means dead" logic entirely.** Don't keep it as a fallback.
- **Optionally stop a failed rebuild from leaving the box containerless**, if that turns out to be a clean change.
- **Write an ADR first.** This reverses ADR 0022 §4, which says the reaper stays unchanged, so the prompt asks for a Proposed ADR before the code, plus DESIGN.md updates. It also asks for tests: a failed, containerless box keeps its data indefinitely; a folder whose sandbox isn't on the list is deleted after the grace period; no list means nothing is deleted.
